summary:
Kuyavian-Pomeranian Voivodeship stands under Poland's national framework on gender identity and sexual orientation. The sources identify no voivodeship-specific statute, court practice or detention-facility rule departing from it, so the national standards set out below are what a trans visitor here actually faces.

Detention is the clearest documented risk to a trans visitor in Poland. On 13 March 2024 the Association for Legal Intervention reported that a regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman, on hormone therapy since 2018, in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. Polish law bars placement in such a centre wherever a stay would threaten the person's life or health, or wherever the person shows signs of having suffered violence. The Border Guard refused to move or release her despite that bar; she was released only after the association applied to the Border Guard Post commander, and the association updated its case page on 28 March 2024. The same case documented a history of violence and sexual assault. Because the case turns on national immigration-detention law, any trans visitor detained in this voivodeship is held under these rules and this pattern of enforcement.

Courts have proved willing to intervene on custody care. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans woman hormone-replacement therapy in Siedlce prison, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages. The Court held the refusal had no reasonable legal grounds and was disproportionate, and left the alleged breaches of Articles 3 and 14 undecided. The judgment binds Poland as a whole and is the governing standard for trans healthcare in Polish prisons and detention in every voivodeship, including Kuyavian-Pomeranian. Poland operates no specialised trans prison section, and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities: Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days. The same advisory lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status.

The wider legal environment is in transition. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk as slow and insufficient through 2024. Deputy Justice Minister Krzysztof Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 Justice Minister Adam Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Zbigniew Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.
tangentialFactors:
The detention case and the prison ruling concern two different custody systems: immigration detention for foreigners under the Border Guard, and criminal custody under the prison service. Both are governed nationally, so a trans visitor's exposure depends on which system holds them rather than on where in Poland they are held.

The gap between the statutory bar on placing a person in a male guarded centre and the Border Guard's initial refusal to apply it shows that written protection and frontline practice diverge; NGO intervention was needed to obtain release.

The European Court of Human Rights has twice ruled against Poland on LGBT-related grounds within four months of each other, in July 2024 on prison healthcare and in September 2024 on the absence of partnership recognition. Both rulings bind Poland nationally.

Pending hate-speech and Penal Code amendments would raise penalties for anti-LGBTI speech and violence. Their status at the time of travel should be verified rather than assumed, since approval of the March draft was postponed and a second bill followed in late October 2024.

Global Affairs Canada couples its visa-free entry note with a harassment advisory citing sexual orientation, physical appearance and foreigner status as reported motives, which places trans visitors at the intersection of two of the listed motives.
localsOnly:
Residents of Kuyavian-Pomeranian Voivodeship live under the same national rules as visitors on detention placement, prison healthcare and hate-crime protection, with the additional exposure that follows from ordinary residence rather than a stay of up to 90 days.

Since June 2024 marriage certificates obtained abroad by same-sex couples are recognised following Justice Minister Adam Bodnar's revocation of Zbigniew Ziobro's blocking directive, while no partnership framework existed domestically as of the September 2024 European Court of Human Rights ruling.

Residents share the enforcement environment described in the detention case: the statutory bar on harmful placement applies, but compliance has depended on external pressure applied to the Border Guard.

The special response team and law-enforcement guidelines issued by the Prosecutor General, together with any enacted hate-speech provisions, shape how residents' complaints of anti-LGBTI crime are handled locally.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not identify any Kuyavian-Pomeranian Voivodeship statute, voivodeship court practice or local detention-facility rule on gender identity; the record rests entirely on the national framework, and no local departure is documented either way.

Whether the Siedlce prison ruling has changed medication supply in facilities serving this voivodeship is not sourced here; the judgment binds Poland but no implementation data is available in the inventory.

The final status of the March and October 2024 hate-speech and Penal Code bills is unresolved in the sources and should be checked against current legislation before travel.

No voivodeship-level data on anti-trans violence, police response times or access to gender-affirming care is available in this inventory; the harassment and care findings derive from national and international reporting.

The Canadian advisory's harassment motives are reported rather than quantified, and no incidence figures for Kuyavian-Pomeranian Voivodeship are sourced.
